summary: Describes Data Link Switching, a way to carry link-layer traffic such as SNA and NetBIOS across a TCP/IP network between switches. It is an informational document produced by an industry group rather than a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some older computer systems cannot talk over the Internet directly. This describes a method of wrapping their messages so they can travel through it anyway.

questions: how does dlsw work over tcp/ip
subtitle: How IBM SNA and NetBIOS traffic is carried between data link switches over TCP/IP, with the link layer terminated locally.

tldr.problem: SNA and NetBIOS use connection-oriented link-layer procedures (LLC Type 2) that were designed for a local LAN, and they misbehave over slow, variable-delay wide area links when simply bridged.
tldr.mechanism: Data Link Switches end the link-layer connection locally and carry the frames between them over TCP using the Switch-to-Switch Protocol (SSP), which has its own message types, circuits, capabilities exchange and flow control.
tldr.outcome: This version 1 standard replaces RFC 1434. It is informational, was produced by an industry group, and says nothing about security.

today: RFC 1795 is an informational document that obsoletes RFC 1434. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: What Data Link Switching Is
sections.content:
Data Link Switching (DLSw) is a forwarding mechanism for IBM's SNA (Systems Network Architecture) and NetBIOS protocols. This memo documents the Switch-to-Switch Protocol (SSP) used between data link switches. DLSw does not provide full routing. It switches at the SNA data link layer and encapsulates frames in TCP/IP for transport. The initial implementation uses TCP, though the text notes that other transports such as OSI TP4 could be used in future.

A switch can support SNA systems (PU 2, PU 2.1 and PU 4) and optionally NetBIOS systems on IEEE 802.2 LANs, as well as SNA systems on SDLC links. SDLC-attached systems are given a LAN appearance, and for Token-Ring systems the switch appears as a source-routing bridge with a virtual ring inside each switch.

The memo was produced by the DLSw Related Interest Group of the APPN Implementers Workshop, a group sponsored by IBM, to give vendors a single version of the protocol, fix documentation problems in RFC 1434, and extend it. It deliberately does not say how to interoperate with RFC 1434 or its enhanced variants.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two post offices that pass letters for a club whose members only trust local mail. Each post office takes the letter locally and sends it to the other one in a sturdy package.

sections.title: Why Not Just Bridge?
sections.content:
SNA and NetBIOS are basically connection oriented and use IEEE 802.2 LLC Type 2 on the LAN. LLC Type 2 assumes predictable network delay and uses a fixed timer to detect lost frames. Over wide area lines the delay is larger and varies with congestion. If the delay exceeds the time-out, the sender retransmits, the procedures can become confused, and the link may eventually be taken down.

DLSw addresses these bridging problems: link control time-outs, acknowledgments over the WAN, flow and congestion control, broadcast control of search packets, and source-route bridging hop count limits.

The key difference is that for connection-oriented data, DLSw terminates the data link control while a bridge does not. LLC Type 2 connections do not cross the wide area network, so time-outs and acknowledgments (RRs) stay on the local LAN, SDLC polling is local, and TCP guarantees delivery between the switches. Switches can also apply back pressure to end systems. DLSw multiplexes many LLC connections onto a TCP connection to another switch.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter to a friend far away needed a thumbs-up for every word, it would be slow. Here the nearby post office gives the thumbs-up right away and the sturdy package handles the long trip.

sections.title: Transport Connections and SSP Messages
sections.content:
Before switching can happen, two routers establish two TCP connections, one for each direction. The default parameters are socket family AF_INET, type SOCK_STREAM, read port 2065 and write port 2067. After connecting, the switches exchange SSP messages to learn each other's capabilities, then use SSP control messages to set up end-to-end circuits.

There are two header formats. Control messages use a 72-byte header. Information messages (INFOFRAME), keepalives and independent flow control messages use a 16-byte header. The first 16 bytes are identical in both. The Version Number is 0x31, the Protocol ID is 0x42, and the Frame Direction is 0x01 from origin to target and 0x02 from target to origin.

A data link is identified by a 14-byte Data Link ID made of the target and origin MAC address (6 bytes) and link SAP (1 byte) pairs. A circuit is identified by a pair of Circuit IDs, each 8 bytes made of a 4-byte DLC Port ID and a 4-byte Data Link Correlator, assigned locally. Correlator and transport ID values have local significance only and are echoed back unchanged.

The Largest Frame Size field lets the two ends agree on a frame size so the switches do not have to re-segment frames. Unknown message types are quietly dropped without terminating the transport connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message wears a label with the same first part, like a header on every envelope, and some envelopes carry a longer label with extra address details for setting up a conversation.

sections.title: Starting and Running a Circuit
sections.content:
An end-to-end circuit is set up with a three-way exchange. The origin switch sends CANUREACH_cs, the target replies ICANREACH_cs with its Target Circuit ID, and the origin answers REACH_ACK with its Origin Circuit ID. Both sides are then in the circuit established state. Explorer versions of the first two messages (_ex, marked by the SSPex flag) only find a remote address without creating a circuit.

Next come XIDFRAME messages, then CONTACT and CONTACTED, after which both sides are connected and data flows in INFOFRAME messages with the shorter header. The behavior of each circuit is defined as a state machine with thirteen states, starting in DISCONNECTED and settling in CIRCUIT_ESTABLISHED or CONNECTED. Separate state machines cover NetBIOS name queries and explorer traffic.

Each circuit also has a priority chosen at start: the initiator and target each propose one in CANUREACH_cs and ICANREACH_cs, and the initiator fixes the value in REACH_ACK for the life of the circuit. Restart and disconnect use RESTART_DL, DL_RESTARTED, HALT_DL and DL_HALTED.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a phone call: first you ask whether the person can be reached, they say yes, you confirm, you say hello, and only then do you start talking.

sections.title: Capabilities and Flow Control
sections.content:
The first SSP message on a new transport connection is the capabilities exchange (CAP_EXCHANGE, type 0x20), which is required. It carries control vectors such as Vendor Id, DLSw Version, Initial Pacing Window, MAC address and NetBIOS name lists, and the number of TCP connections. Vector identifiers 0x80 to 0xCF are reserved for the standard and 0xD0 to 0xFD for vendor-specific use. The Version vector reports version 1, release 0.

Flow control is done per circuit and per direction with adaptive pacing. A sender may send only as many data units (DGRMFRAME or INFOFRAME) as its receiver has granted. The receiver grants permission with a Flow Control Indicator and the sender confirms with a Flow Control Acknowledgment, carried in the one-byte flow control field at offset 15. Five operators adjust the window: repeat, increment, decrement, reset and halve.

Protocol violations include exceeding granted units, leaving a Reset Window operator without a following Increment, and growing the window past 0xFFFF. What to do about a violation is left to the implementation, though HALT_DL is the appropriate action if the circuit is taken down. The older enter-busy and exit-busy messages are not used in this standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver hands the sender a few tickets at a time. The sender can only send as many messages as it has tickets, so nobody gets flooded.

viz.caption: FIRST 16 BYTES SHARED BY ALL SSP HEADERS (RFC 1795)

fields.name: Header Length
fields.desc: 0x48 (72) for control messages, 0x10 (16) for information messages.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Number of bytes in the data field after the header.

fields.name: Remote Data Link Correlator
fields.desc: Identifies the circuit at the remote switch.

fields.name: Remote DLC Port ID
fields.desc: Identifies the DLC port at the remote switch.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: Identifies the SSP message, for example 0x0A for INFOFRAME.

fields.name: Flow Control Byte
fields.desc: Flow control indicator, acknowledgment and operator bits.

viz.caption: CIRCUIT STARTUP BETWEEN TWO DATA LINK SWITCHES (RFC 1795)

messages.label: CANUREACH_cs
messages.note: Can you reach this station? Carries the Data Link ID.

messages.label: ICANREACH_cs
messages.note: Yes. Includes the Target Circuit ID.

messages.label: REACH_ACK
messages.note: Includes the Origin Circuit ID; circuit established.

messages.label: XIDFRAME
messages.note: XID frames can flow in both directions.

messages.label: CONTACT
messages.note: Asks the target to contact the remote station.

items.label: Repeat Window
items.desc: Window unchanged; grant a further window of units.

items.label: Increment Window
items.desc: Grow the window by one, then grant it.

items.label: Decrement Window
items.desc: Shrink the window by one; only if window is greater than one.

items.label: Reset Window
items.desc: Window and granted units go to zero; sent on its own, never piggy-backed.

items.label: Halve Window
items.desc: Halve the window if it is greater than one, then grant it.
